source: Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan (2010) The weirdest people in the world? BBS 33
finding: Behavioral science samples come almost entirely from WEIRD societies, so claims about 'people' rest on a thin slice.
numbers: Arnett 2008 count: 68% of subjects from the US, 96% from Western industrialized countries (12% of world population). 67% of US samples in JPSP were psychology undergraduates (80% outside the US). Claimed odds: a US undergraduate is over 4,000 times more likely to be a participant than a random non-Westerner.
limits: Counts are for top journals 2003-2007; a base rate, not a test of any one effect.
agent_relevance: Weight any 'humans do X' result by who was sampled. A model trained on this literature inherits the skew.

source: Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan (2010) The weirdest people in the world? BBS 33
finding: Analytic vs holistic reasoning is not only an East-West split. Westerners look like the outlier among many groups.
numbers: Cited: Witkin & Berry (1975): only Westerners and migratory foragers sit at the field-independent end on Rod and Frame and Embedded Figures. Norenzayan 2007: Canadians less field-dependent than Chinese, who are less than Arabs. Mapuche (Chile) and Sangu (Tanzania) farmers sorted objects like Chinese, even more holistic.
limits: Review of other people's studies; some cited as unpublished. Not a new test.
agent_relevance: Treat 'analytic, rule-first, decontextualized' as one regional style, not the default of reasoning.

source: Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan (2010) The weirdest people in the world? BBS 33
finding: Cultural variation is large for some processes and absent for others. The Muller-Lyer illusion shows the range.
numbers: Segall et al. 1966: 16 societies (14 small-scale); illusion size (point of subjective equality) varied and could not be detected in two populations. US undergraduates sit at the extreme end.
limits: Visual perception, not reasoning. Shows 'universal or variable' must be tested per task.
agent_relevance: Per-task evidence is needed. No blanket claim that reasoning is universal or variable.

source: Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan (2010) The weirdest people in the world? BBS 33
finding: Self-construal is proposed as a driver of analytic vs holistic style, and primes shift style inside one person.
numbers: Oyserman & Lee 2008: independent primes raise analytic processing, interdependent primes raise holistic. Varnum 2008: regions with more interdependence are more holistic (N vs S Italy, Hokkaido vs mainland Japan, W vs E Europe).
limits: Priming effects have a mixed replication record (see sibling subfield 07).
agent_relevance: If style is a switchable bias, a scaffold may set it by prompt. Test, do not assume.

source: Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan (2010) The weirdest people in the world? BBS 33
finding: The fundamental attribution error is weaker outside the US. Chinese, Japanese and Russians weigh the situation more, especially when it is salient.
numbers: Church et al. 2006, eight populations: US and Euro-Australian endorse stable traits strongly; Asian-Australian, Chinese-Malaysian, Filipino, Japanese, Mexican and Malay endorse situational beliefs more.
limits: Endorsement and judgment tasks. Choi et al. 1999 note dispositional inference still exists outside the West.
agent_relevance: Strong dispositional attribution in LLM output reflects one cultural default.

source: Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan (2010) The weirdest people in the world? BBS 33
finding: Rival view in the commentary: common processes can be universal while their expression differs by culture.
numbers: Example: self-enhancement on valued attributes (individualist traits in the West, collectivist traits in the East) with the same link to adjustment in both groups (Sedikides, Gaertner, Brown cited).
limits: Commentary argument; evidence cited, not retested here.
agent_relevance: Supports one shared reasoning engine with context-specific defaults, which matches our guardrail design.

source: Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan (2010) The weirdest people in the world? BBS 33
finding: A commentator tested broadening through the Internet: 564,502 participants answered a personality survey, still not representative.
numbers: 19% not from advanced economies; 20% non-Western; 35% of the Western sample not from the US; 66% of the US sample outside college age (18-22).
limits: Commentary abstract, not an effect test. Internet samples skew rich and online.
agent_relevance: Large data sets can fix age skew but not culture skew. Our training data has the same issue.

source: Norenzayan, Smith, Kim & Nisbett (2002) Cultural preferences for formal versus intuitive reasoning (author manuscript, Cognitive Science)
finding: Founding design: culture differences appear only when a formal rule and intuition are put in conflict. Under a classification instruction there was no difference.
numbers: Study 2 (52 European Americans, 52 Asian Americans, 53 East Asians; Michigan undergraduates). Classification instruction: all groups chose the rule 67% vs 33% family resemblance, culture x response F(2,100)=1.25 ns. Similarity instruction: European Americans 69% rule vs 31%; East Asians 41% vs 59%; Asian Americans 46% vs 54%; interaction F(2,51)=8.01, p<.005. Only 18 per group in the similarity cell.
limits: Small cells; instruction decides the outcome; English-language tasks given to US university students.
agent_relevance: Instruction wording switches reasoning style within a group. State the criterion (rule vs similarity) explicitly in agent prompts.

source: Norenzayan, Smith, Kim & Nisbett (2002) Cultural preferences for formal versus intuitive reasoning (author manuscript, Cognitive Science)
finding: Study 3: Koreans were more swayed by argument typicality than European Americans, but only when typicality was not salient and logic was available.
numbers: Low-salience arguments: culture x argument type F(2,253)=4.67, p<.01; typicality effect larger in Koreans than European Americans F(1,253)=9.09. European Americans showed no typicality effect t(90)=1.16 ns; Koreans t(91)=5.98. Within-subject version: all groups rated typical conclusions higher (Korean typical M=8.49 vs atypical 5.00). High salience: no culture difference.
limits: The interaction vanished when typicality was made salient. Translated by back-translation.
agent_relevance: The intuition-vs-logic gap is a default under low cue salience; making the cue explicit removes it.

source: Norenzayan, Smith, Kim & Nisbett (2002) Cultural preferences for formal versus intuitive reasoning (author manuscript, Cognitive Science)
finding: Study 4, belief bias in syllogisms: Koreans showed more belief bias on valid arguments, but there was also a response bias, so part of the effect is not reasoning.
numbers: 3-way interaction culture x validity x believability F(1,184)=4.73, p<.05; belief bias larger for Koreans only on valid arguments; Koreans less likely to say 'yes' overall F(1,184)=14.41. Both groups strongly sensitive to validity F(1,184)=1161.73.
limits: Response-bias confound. The difference is small next to the shared validity sensitivity.
agent_relevance: Both groups reason logically; cultures differ in the tie-break when logic and belief clash. Universal engine, variable defaults.

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2: Investigating variation in replicability across samples and settings. AMPPS 1(4)
finding: Large preregistered multi-site test of 28 findings. Effects shrank, but site and setting heterogeneity was small.
numbers: 28 findings, 125 samples, 15,305 participants, 36 countries. 54% (15/28) significant at p<.05, 50% at p<.0001. Median d 0.60 original vs 0.15 replication. 32% (9) in the opposite direction. Q heterogeneity significant in 39%. Per Schimmelpfennig, only 3 of 28 effects were moderated by the WEIRD split.
limits: Abstract read through the Crossref record, not the full text. Culture test was exploratory. Samples mostly WEIRD.
agent_relevance: Original effect sizes are inflated about 4x at the median. Discount them when setting evidence weights.

source: Schimmelpfennig, Spicer, White, Gervais, Norenzayan, Heine, Henrich & Muthukrishna (2024) Methodological concerns underlying a lack of evidence for cultural heterogeneity in the replication of psychological effects. Communications Psychology 2:93
finding: The Many Labs 2 conclusion of 'little cultural variation' is a power and sampling artifact, not proof of universality.
numbers: ML2 average cultural distance from the US (CFST) 0.062 by participant, 0.055 by site, less than US-Germany (0.069); 91% of sites below 0.15 while the world range reaches about 0.3. Power to detect cultural moderation 28% even for strong influence; under 8% for some effects. Moderation found in 3/28 (11%), which fits a world where culture influence is at least moderate. 409 citing papers screened.
limits: Authors include Norenzayan, Heine and Henrich (interested parties). Their re-analysis with continuous cultural distance raised effect sizes only slightly and did not overturn ML2.
agent_relevance: Absence of a significant culture effect in a WEIRD-heavy set is weak evidence for universals.

source: Schimmelpfennig, Spicer, White, Gervais, Norenzayan, Heine, Henrich & Muthukrishna (2024) Methodological concerns underlying a lack of evidence for cultural heterogeneity in the replication of psychological effects. Communications Psychology 2:93
finding: The ML2 replication of Norenzayan 2002 Study 2 changed the design: the original used matched US college students, ML2 spread it across countries.
numbers: Paper says the original found differences in a standardized sample 'matched based on cognitive abilities and education', while ML2 expanded to country variation without that logic. Norenzayan 2002 was one of the 3 of 28 moderated by ML2-WEIRDness.
limits: The ML2 effect size for this study was not retrieved (Norenzayan's commentary was paywalled).
agent_relevance: A replication that changes the comparison population is not a clean test. Check design equivalence before treating it as a refutation.

source: Hakim, Simons, Zhao & Wan (2017) Do Easterners and Westerners differ in visual cognition? A preregistered examination of three visual cognition tasks. SPPS
finding: A preregistered, larger-sample replication of classic holistic/analytic perception tasks found little robust or consistent difference.
numbers: Tasks: global/local bias, relative vs absolute length (framed-line), change detection. American vs Asian international students in the US. 'Relatively little evidence' of robust differences; some change-detection differences for Chinese vs American students were inconsistent across measures. Exact N not retrieved.
limits: Abstract only. Asian international students in the US are a selected group. Authors call for controls on test context and demand characteristics.
agent_relevance: Perceptual East-West contrasts are fragile. Do not build scaffold rules on them.

source: Mercier, Zhang, Qu, Lu & Yama (2015) Do Easterners and Westerners treat contradiction differently? J Cognition and Culture 15
finding: Failed replication and new test of Peng and Nisbett (1999) naive dialecticism: Chinese and French participants behaved similarly.
numbers: Two Peng & Nisbett experiments re-tested with alternative interpretations, plus a third new test. Chinese and French groups 'behaved similarly', not showing the original differences. Exact N and effect sizes not retrieved.
limits: Abstract only. French rather than American comparison group. Authors cite earlier failed replications as well.
agent_relevance: Dialectical-reasoning claims (sibling 02) carry low weight. Do not code 'accept contradiction' as an East Asian mode.

source: Rad, Martingano & Ginges (2018) Toward a psychology of Homo sapiens. PNAS 115
finding: Audit of Psychological Science finds WEIRD reliance almost total, with unreflective generalization to humans.
numbers: Abstract: 'almost all research' in the journal relies on Western samples and generalizes without qualification. Exact percentages not retrieved.
limits: Abstract only; full text blocked.
agent_relevance: The evidence base for any claim in our schema is biased toward the same samples.

source: Talhelm, Zhang, Oishi, Shimin, Duan, Lan & Kitayama (2014) Large-scale psychological differences within China explained by rice versus wheat agriculture. Science 344
finding: Within-China contrast: rice vs wheat farming regions differ on holistic and collectivist tasks, which points to an ecological cause and weakens the 'East' label.
numbers: Three cognitive measures, about 1,000 subjects from rice and wheat regions (abstract). Effect sizes not retrieved.
limits: Abstract only. A search in this session found no independent replication of the rice theory.
agent_relevance: Style may follow livelihood, not nation: another reason not to key agent behavior to a country label.

source: Jin et al. (2023) The Cultural Psychology of Large Language Models: Is ChatGPT a Holistic or Analytic Thinker? arXiv 2308.14242
finding: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 score more holistic than human norms on analysis-holism scales, but not consistently on value scales.
numbers: 10 runs per model at temperature 1. Analysis-Holism Scale: GPT-3.5 M=5.35 (SD 0.11), GPT-4 5.01 (0.10) vs human norm 4.87 (SD 0.49, N=702), both p<.001. Dialectical Self: GPT-3.5 4.59 vs norm 4.00 (N=158); GPT-4 3.97 ns (p=.344). Independent self-construal: GPT-3.5 6.98, GPT-4 5.32 vs norm 4.73 (N=382), both p<.001. Triadic categorization: GPT-3.5 0.87, GPT-4 0.85, above most Chinese provinces.
limits: Self-report scales given to a model. Ten runs with tiny SD make t-tests overstate. Holistic on cognition scales yet individualist on self scales.
agent_relevance: LLM 'holism' scores come from agreeing with items, not from reasoning behavior. Do not treat scale answers as style evidence.

source: Jin et al. (2023) The Cultural Psychology of Large Language Models: Is ChatGPT a Holistic or Analytic Thinker? arXiv 2308.14242
finding: Design critique: the main cognitive-process measures lacked a matched human norm, and runs were few.
numbers: Triadic categorization had no norm, only provincial Chinese means; norms came from different studies (N=702, 158, 382); N=10 runs per cell. Authors say results held across temperature and prompt-language changes.
limits: Scale items need self-insight a model lacks, as the authors admit.
agent_relevance: Single-source (S). Weak evidence.

source: Hu, Peng, Zhao, Qiu, Hung & Peng (2026) Beyond instrumental and substitutive paradigms: machine culture. arXiv 2601.17096
finding: 2x2 test (US vs Chinese model x English vs Chinese prompt) did not reproduce human holistic/analytic patterns. Model origin and prompt language did not predict them.
numbers: Image generation: US model (DALL-E 3) made more objects (M=11.53, SD 4.39) than Chinese model (iRAG, 8.10, SD 1.91), t=-10.14, p<.001, d=1.01; horizon higher 533.5 vs 519.8, d=0.34. Human data predict the reverse. Prompt language: Chinese prompts gave more objects (10.71 vs 8.91, d=0.49) but no horizon difference (523.2 vs 530.1, p=.096, d=0.17).
limits: Eight tasks, two model families; image pipelines also differ in rewriting layers. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Model origin is a poor proxy for cognitive style. A persona label gives unstable effects.

source: Hu, Peng, Zhao, Qiu, Hung & Peng (2026) Beyond instrumental and substitutive paradigms: machine culture. arXiv 2601.17096
finding: 'Cultural reversal': English prompts gave more contextual detail than Chinese prompts in scene interpretation, opposite to the human pattern.
numbers: Object counts in descriptions: English M=10.90 (SD 2.61) vs Chinese M=10.06 (SD 2.02), t(374.94)=-3.60, p<.001, d=0.36. Authors blame English data density. Affect: image generation followed stereotypes (high-arousal positive 113 US vs 79 CN, chi2=28.36; low-arousal positive 41 CN vs 2 US, chi2=40.91), but text tasks collapsed to a hyper-positive assistant persona.
limits: Verbosity confounds 'holistic' counts. Preprint, two models.
agent_relevance: Counting context items rewards verbosity, not holistic reasoning. Use length-controlled measures (as G5 already requires).

source: Hu, Peng, Zhao, Qiu, Hung & Peng (2026) Beyond instrumental and substitutive paradigms: machine culture. arXiv 2601.17096
finding: Related-work claim: concepts across languages share neurons and an English-centric space, so a language switch may not switch 'culture'.
numbers: Cites Lindsey 2025, Templeton 2024 and Wendler 2024 for shared concept sets, and Sclar 2023 and Khan 2025 for prompt-format sensitivity larger than human cultural variation. Not tested in the paper.
limits: Secondary citation; cited papers not checked.
agent_relevance: Format sensitivity of LLMs is a rival explanation for 'cultural' effects. Control for it.

source: Sabir, Gasper, Loem & Sharma (2025) Contrasting cognitive styles in vision-language models. arXiv 2507.00700
finding: Japanese captions start with the background more often than English ones, and Japanese-centric images raise it further.
numbers: GPT-4o judges whether a caption starts with background (holistic) or object (analytic). Holistic %: HERON-BENCH GPT4o 5-shot 25.58, GPT4o-JP 34.88, balanced 6-shot 53.49; JA-VLM 23.81, 38.10, 61.90; 1K-JP images 59.10, 63.86, 73.37.
limits: GPT-4o judges its own family (self-preference risk). 'Holistic' means only the first-mentioned item. The prompt change from 5-shot to balanced 6-shot moves the share 10 to 24 points.
agent_relevance: Prompt design moves the measure more than the 'cultural' signal. Treat as weak evidence.

source: Sabir, Gasper, Loem & Sharma (2025) Contrasting cognitive styles in vision-language models. arXiv 2507.00700
finding: Image content shifts caption style as much as language does, and model size interacts.
numbers: Larger models (GPT-4o-JP, Gemma-27B-JP) more holistic than VILA-JP-14B; VILA-JP gave English-like captions in Japanese on COCO. Japanese datasets raised holistic share versus Western COCO (text: GPT-4o-JP 26.10% on COCO to 73.37% on 1K-JP).
limits: Table 4 and 5 (human check on 200 images) not extracted.
agent_relevance: 'Holism' in captions may just be scene content.

source: Atari, Xue, Park, Blasi & Henrich (2023) Which humans? PsyArXiv 5b26t
finding: LLM answers to psychological measures are an outlier against large cross-cultural data, resemble WEIRD people, and fall off with cultural distance.
numbers: Abstract: correlation between how WEIRD a population is and similarity to GPT output r = -.70. The page opened held the abstract and reference list only; per-task numbers not read.
limits: Abstract and references only. Preprint. GPT family tested.
agent_relevance: When asked about non-WEIRD settings, expect WEIRD defaults and use external checks.

source: Tao, Viberg, Baker & Kizilcec (2024) Cultural bias and cultural alignment of large language models. arXiv 2311.14096
finding: All five GPT models sit near English-speaking and Protestant European values. Cultural prompting helps in most countries but not all.
numbers: Mean distance to survey values without then with cultural prompting: GPT-4o 2.42 to 1.57, GPT-4-turbo 2.71 to 1.77, GPT-4 2.69 to 1.65 (p<.001); GPT-3 2.39 to 2.11, GPT-3.5-turbo 3.35 to 2.83. Improved for 71.0% (4o), 81.3% (4-turbo), 77.6% (4), 72.6% (3.5-turbo), 80.4% (GPT-3) of countries; 19-29% saw no gain or worse. GPT-4o Finland 0.20 to 2.43, Taiwan 2.40 to 3.94.
limits: Value survey on the Inglehart-Welzel map, not reasoning tasks. Ten prompt wordings averaged. Remaining bias 1.57 is about the distance to Uruguay.
agent_relevance: A country prompt shifts values but can overshoot. Do not use persona prompting for reasoning diversity without measuring.

source: AlKhamissi, AlKhamissi, Ahmed & Diab (2024) Investigating cultural alignment of large language models. arXiv 2402.13231
finding: Models align better with Egyptian survey answers when prompted in Arabic and with US answers in English. Pretraining language mix also matters.
numbers: Egypt and US sociological surveys replicated with real-respondent personas, two prompt languages and several pretraining mixes; Table 2 gives soft and hard alignment by prompt language. Exact deltas not extracted.
limits: Abstract and result prose only. Conflicts with Hu 2026, where prompt language gave no stable switching.
agent_relevance: Prompt-language effects disagree across studies. Do not depend on them.
